description: We are all hard-working students from the RTP area trying to develop our skills in computer science and artificial intelligence.
summary:
Clouds cover the Amazon for much of the year, and photo satellites can’t see through them. NISAR’s radar can. We pulled 9 NISAR passes from June to October 2026 over the BR-163 highway near Novo Progresso, Pará, where forest is being cut for cattle pasture, and every one of them was usable. Sentinel-2 had 5 of its 32 photos fully hidden by cloud over the same months.

From those passes we made a forest map with a single radar brightness cut-off. We set it on a small strip and never changed it. Over the whole 57,117 km² radar image it agrees with the Hansen forest map 92.6% of the time (just calling everything “forest” gets 86.2%). Spots that went from forest to open land are 25.7 times more likely than random forest to line up with a GLAD deforestation alert. That still isn’t proof, since only 3.3% of them do.

All of this lives in Amazon Forest Watch, a website where anyone can explore the radar, see where to look first, and read what the method can’t tell you. Our first detector failed, and we say so on the site.
details:
What it does and how it works
Through the Clouds is a website built on NISAR, the NASA-ISRO radar satellite launched in 2025. NISAR uses long-wave L-band radar, so clouds and smoke don’t stop it. We worked on one frontier: the BR-163 highway near Novo Progresso, Pará, Brazil. The radar data is NISAR’s early-release (provisional) L2 GCOV product. We streamed only small windows of each roughly 5 GB file instead of downloading them. That gave us 9 passes from 2026-06-26 to 2026-10-12, never more than 24 days apart.

Forest bounces back a strong cross-polarized (HV) radar signal and cleared ground a weak one. So our forest map is one brightness cut-off on that signal, -11.25 dB. We picked it on the north half of a 20 km test area and froze it. Then we tested it, unchanged, on other areas up to the whole radar image, against the Hansen forest map. Before scoring, we wrote the rules down in pre-registration files in the repo (validation/PREREG_*.md) and scored each area once:

  • south half of the 20 km test area: 83.1% agreement, versus 52.4% if you call everything forest
  • a different area in Rondônia: 95.6% versus 72.7%
  • a 60 km area along BR-163: 95.4% versus 81.3%
  • the whole radar image, 57,117 km²: 92.6% versus 86.2%

Next, we flagged 100 m squares that looked like forest early in the season and like open land on the last two passes. Over the whole image, these flags are 25.7 times more likely than random stable forest to overlap a GLAD-L deforestation alert (3.3% versus 0.13%). That tells us the flags aren’t random. It doesn’t tell us they’re right, because most of them have no alert at all.

On the site you can:

  • move through the radar map for 4 places
  • watch the forest map change pass by pass
  • compare radar with Sentinel-2 photos taken around the same dates
  • see flagged spots inside Indigenous lands, plus the 20 biggest spots to check first
  • open any spot to see its radar history, whether an alert agrees, and NASA FIRMS fire detections near it
  • download the list of spots as GeoJSON or CSV, and a data report with every number on the page

Benefits and intended impact
Over the same months, Sentinel-2 had 5 of 32 photos fully hidden by cloud, while all 9 radar passes gave a usable map. Radar could fill those gaps for the people who already watch this forest with photo-based alert systems. Our flags can tell someone where to send a closer look. They can’t prove clearing on their own, and the site says that next to every result. We wrote the text for a general reader, with a glossary and short “How we know” boxes for the details.

Tools

  • Python 3.13: earthaccess and asf_search to reach NASA Earthdata/ASF, xarray, h5netcdf, h5py and fsspec to stream the HDF5 files, numpy, scipy, scikit-image, rioxarray, rasterio, geopandas and shapely for the processing, matplotlib for plots, pytest for tests
  • Data: NISAR L2 GCOV (provisional), Hansen Global Forest Change v1.13, GLAD-L and GLAD-S2 alerts from the Global Forest Watch API, Sentinel-2 scene classification from Earth Search, NASA FIRMS fire detections, FUNAI Indigenous land boundaries
  • Website: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with MapLibre GL JS, hosted on Vercel, tested with Node and Playwright on desktop and phone sizes
  • Hardware: the data processing ran on our own computers over home internet. No paid cloud computing.

How it’s creative
Many forest alerts come from photos (GLAD uses Landsat and Sentinel-2), and NISAR’s open L2 data is new. We pushed a single fixed threshold from a 20 km test area out to a whole radar image and showed every score next to the “just guess forest” number, so you can see how much the map actually adds. We also put our failures on the site. Our first detector, a JJ-FAST-style change detector with a 1 dB cut-off, matched only 2 of 57 flags to alerts and found 0 of 179 alerts. When we checked 6 of its flags by hand in Sentinel-2 photos, none showed clearing. It’s still on the site, marked “did not work”.

What we considered

  • The data is provisional. We found problems in it: in Rondônia the 2026-07-12 image was scaled wrong (its mean_value attribute is 576.8 instead of about 0.22), and three early dates didn’t show the same ground as the later ones. We left those dates out and reported both problems.
  • Hansen and GLAD come from photos and have their own errors. We call them “other maps to compare with”, not ground truth.
  • We only have the dry season (June to October). Late in that season the radar sees forest as less forest-like, so many flags are probably seasonal drying..
  • The method can’t see selective logging, fire or flooding.
  • We don’t claim this stops deforestation, saves carbon, or works everywhere.
